rule: Top warm-up bar speed <= -10% vs the 6-week median -> cap main-lift load at last week's (~-3%)
summary: Velocity against a fixed load is a validated fatigue marker: it is depressed for 6-24 h after demanding squat sessions and tracks relative load tightly, so a clear drop signals reduced capacity. A 10% drop is beyond typical measurement error, so the threshold is reasonably specific; the response (hold last week's load) is mild. The specific 10% is not tested anywhere, and velocity of near-maximal loads is unreliable, so it should be applied to a submaximal warm-up load as the code does.

sources.note: Velocity against the 1 m/s load fell after high-fatigue squat protocols and stayed down up to 24 h - velocity detects residual fatigue
Higher velocity-loss protocols impaired V1-load at 6-24 h; velocity at a fixed load used as recovery marker
Typical error 0.6-8.8% - a 10% drop is mostly beyond noise
Velocity at 1RM was unreliable (CV 22.5%) - use submaximal warm-up velocity, not near-max sets
Review: VBT is an objective way to address daily readiness; supplements, not replaces, coach judgement
